sections.normalized_html:
We are told that [MATH: h(x) = 5 \cdot 2^x] and that [MATH: k(x) = h(x + 3).]

To find the equation for [MATH: k(x),] we substitute [MATH: x+3] into the definition of [MATH: h(x)] wherever [MATH: x] appears. By doing this, we get [MATH: k(x) = h(x + 3) = 5 \cdot 2^{x + 3}.]

Now, we simplify and obtain [MATH: k(x)|= 5 ⋅ 2^{x + 3}; = 5 ⋅ 2^{x} ⋅ 2^{3}; = 5 ⋅ 2^{3} ⋅ 2^{x}; = 5 ⋅ 8 ⋅ 2^{x}; = 40 ⋅ 2^{x}.]

Therefore, the equation that defines [MATH: k] is [MATH: k(x) = 40 \cdot 2^x.]

sections.readable_text: The function [MATH: p] is defined by the equation [MATH: p(x) = 150 \cdot 10^x.] If [MATH: q(x) = p(x - 2),]find the equation that defines the function [MATH: q.]

sections.normalized_html:
We are told that [MATH: p(x) = 150 \cdot 10^x] and that [MATH: q(x) = p(x - 2).]

To find the equation for [MATH: q(x),] we substitute [MATH: x-2] into the definition of [MATH: p(x)] wherever [MATH: x] appears. By doing this, we get [MATH: q(x) = p(x-2) = 150 \cdot 10^{x-2}.]

Now, we simplify and obtain [MATH: q(x)|= 150 ⋅ 10^{x − 2}; = 150 ⋅ 10^{x} ⋅ 10^{− 2}; = 150 ⋅ 10^{− 2} ⋅ 10^{x}; = 150 ⋅ (1)/(100) ⋅ 10^{x}; = (150)/(100) ⋅ 10^{x}; = (3)/(2) ⋅ 10^{x}.]

Therefore, the equation that defines [MATH: q] is [MATH: q(x) = \dfrac{3}{2} \cdot 10^x.]
